objections.text: The stated equivalence is not established: if proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood, then lacking proper parts entails that any parthood relation involving God is symmetric, not that God is a part of every one of God’s parts. Symmetry permits mutual parthood where a relation exists; it does not create parthood relations to all alleged parts.

Modelling instantiation as parthood is highly contentious and does not establish that an object literally has its properties as parts. Even if objects can be described as fusions of properties in one metaphysical framework, God’s omniscience may be identical with God, grounded in God’s nature, or predicated without being a constituent. Thus the parthood model cannot support the proposed symmetry formulation of divine simplicity.

The mere fact that an object can be described as a fusion of its properties does not establish that instantiation is parthood. Properties may be instantiated by an object without being literal constituents of it, so the proposed mereological model requires independent justification.

The unstated premise equivocates between ordinary parthood and similarity-based parthood. Even if absence of proper parts entails that any part relation involving God is symmetric, it does not follow that divine simplicity is the substantive thesis that God is part of all of God’s parts; that formulation may be vacuous, admit distinct mutual parts, and fail to capture the intended claim that God has no metaphysically distinct constituents.

The premise assumes that source attribution necessarily requires a first-personal mode of presentation. But divine cognition could non-indexically and exhaustively represent the fact that God actualises W1 rather than W0, while still grounding responsibility; the relevant issue is whether the cognition correctly represents the agent as the causal source, not whether it contains irreducible de se content.

The premise overstates what responsibility requires. An agent may robustly bring about an outcome through cognition that represents the relevant causal role descriptively—for example, as ‘the being who actualises W1’—without representing that outcome under an irreducibly first-personal ‘my action’ mode of presentation. Causal control and contrastive authorship do not by themselves establish a de se requirement.

The premise equivocates between being the metaphysical source of an outcome and cognitively representing that outcome under a first-personal, de se mode of presentation. An agent could robustly and contrastively control which world is actualised through complete third-personal knowledge of the relevant alternatives and a decisive volitional state, even if no irreducible de se content is involved. Source attribution may be a fact about the causal or agential structure, not a representational condition on the agent's cognition.

Robust contrastive responsibility need not require a first-personal or de se representation of the outcome's source. An agent could deliberately actualise W1 rather than W0 while representing the relevant source through a uniquely identifying, third-personal description—for example, as 'the being with these powers and reasons'—so long as that representation reliably guides its control of the choice. Responsibility depends on authorship and control, not on the irreducible linguistic or cognitive mode under which the agent identifies itself.

The premise treats both worldviews as equally explanatory merely because each can accommodate apparent randomness. But an explanation that invokes hidden providence and delayed judgment may be compatible with any possible distribution of suffering, making it less testable than naturalistic causal accounts. Equal compatibility does not establish equal evidential support, so worldly randomness could still count against biblical theology even if it does not conclusively refute it.

The premise wrongly treats the rival accounts as equally explanatory merely because each can accommodate apparent randomness. A worldview that invokes hidden providence and delayed judgment can be made compatible with virtually any distribution of suffering, but that flexibility weakens its evidential force; naturalistic impersonal causation may generate more specific, independently testable expectations. Thus worldly randomness may still favor one worldview over the other.

Calling hidden providence an explanation does not make it evidentially comparable to naturalism: if every conceivable distribution of suffering is compatible with inscrutable divine purposes, biblical theology supplies no risky prediction or independent criterion for identifying providence. Its compatibility with apparent randomness therefore cannot establish an evidential tie.

The premise wrongly treats symmetric interpretability as evidential parity. A worldview that accommodates morally indiscriminate suffering by appealing to hidden providence and deferred justice may be compatible with the evidence, but compatibility is not an explanation with equal predictive or evidential support. If naturalism expects impersonal, non-morally-directed distributions of suffering more directly than biblical theism does, worldly randomness can still favor naturalism.

The unstated premise simply stipulates that the many-goods conditions remain sufficient even when every good is available within relationship with God. But if those goods can be realized without nonresistant nonbelief, they provide no reason to permit that nonbelief; their collective value cannot establish that the world containing it is more valuable.

The unstated premise equivocates between goods being realizable within a relationship with God and being realizable to the same extent without losing their value. If every identified good can occur within such a relationship, then nonresistant nonbelief is not necessary for those goods; merely aggregating goods that are available without it does not show that their presence compensates for the evil of nonresistant nonbelief.

If every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God, then their realization does not require nonresistant nonbelief. Their mere multiplicity and aggregate value therefore cannot show that a world containing such nonbelief is more valuable than the available alternative without it; the premise simply assumes away the relevant accommodation comparison.

If every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God, then nonresistant nonbelief is not needed to secure any of those goods. Counting several such goods does not make their production through nonbelief justified; the accommodation strategy defeats the response by providing a world with the same goods and the relationship without that evil.

This premise presents a false dilemma: Schellenberg’s conditional premise need not be established only through the a priori conceptual route or Vanstone-based analogy. It may instead be supported by broader moral, experiential, and relational considerations about what a perfectly loving God would reasonably make available to nonresistant persons.

The unstated premise sets an unjustifiably stringent success condition. Schellenberg need not establish the conditional premise exclusively through either an a priori conceptual argument or Vanstone-based analogy; it could be supported by cumulative moral, experiential, or theological considerations. Likewise, showing that belief is not strictly necessary for every meaningful relationship with God does not by itself refute the claim that reasonable belief is normally expected in relationships with a perfectly loving God. Thus the alleged vulnerabilities do not entail that the hiddenness argument is unsuccessful.

This premise sets an unduly strict success condition. Schellenberg’s conditional premise need not be established exclusively by either the a priori conceptual route or the stated analogy; it may be supported by cumulative moral, experiential, and relational considerations. Likewise, even if explicit belief is not necessary for every meaningful relation to God, it may still be necessary for the kind of reciprocal, consciously available relationship relevant to the hiddenness argument. Therefore, the alleged vulnerabilities do not entail that the argument is unsuccessful.

This premise wrongly treats the a priori and analogical arguments as the only possible support for Schellenberg’s conditional premise. Even if both particular routes fail, the conditional might be established by other theological, experiential, or moral considerations; thus their failure does not by itself entail that the hiddenness argument is unsuccessful.

A theology class uses a similarity relation: two things count as mutual parts when each shares every relevant feature with the other. God knows every truth, including that the library is closed. Omniscience is the property of knowing every truth. God and omniscience therefore match on the stipulated knowledge-related features, so the class labels them mutual similarity-parts. Yet they remain numerically distinct: God is an agent who intends to create a world and can answer a prayer; omniscience is a property that neither intends nor answers. The similarity-based mutual-part label does not make the property an entity or preserve a genuine parthood relation. It merely records feature overlap under a coarse rule. Thus mutual similarity does not establish that God and omniscience are parts of one another while distinct.

Mara owns a red apple. The apple is red, round, and five centimeters wide. A curator makes a catalogue entry listing those properties, but the entry is not a physical ingredient of the apple, and neither redness nor roundness is an object that occupies a region inside it. Mara slices the apple: each slice remains red and round, yet no slice contains “the apple’s redness” as a detachable constituent. The apple has properties because it instantiates them; it is not a fusion whose members are those properties. Treating instantiation as parthood therefore confuses predication with composition.

In a theology where God has no proper parts, God is numerically identical with each divine attribute: omniscience is not a distinct constituent but God understood under the description “knows all truths.” Parthood is defined in the ordinary non-symmetric way: x is a proper part of y only if x is part of y and x is not identical with y. Since God has no proper parts, there are no entities satisfying “God’s parts.” The universal claim that God is part of all God’s parts is then vacuously true, even if God is not part of any distinct attribute or constituent. It therefore does not state symmetry, mutual inclusion, or any substantive account of divine simplicity; it is true merely because the relevant domain is empty.

Naturalism treats properties as features grounded in physical structures, dispositions, and lawful patterns, not as independently existing items available for fusion. Consider a neuroscientist who studies a carbon-based organism, Mira. Mira believes that her visual acuity, metabolism, and mass are properties of her organism. After Mira loses visual acuity through retinal damage, the organism persists; its molecules, causal organization, and identity remain continuous, although one attributed property changes. No property departed as a detachable component, and no fusion lost a constituent. The property description tracked a changed physical capacity of the organism. Likewise, an electron’s charge and mass describe its role in physical laws; they are not parts that compose an electron. Treating objects as fusions of properties reverses the naturalist dependence relation: properties are abstractions or physically grounded aspects of objects, whereas objects are concrete causal systems.

In a world-selection system, God has complete propositional knowledge of every possible world and a standing rule: actualise the world with the greatest balance of freely chosen love. God evaluates W0 and W1 through the proposition “the being who actualises W1 thereby makes W1 actual.” God knows that he is that being because the proposition uniquely identifies its subject, and he intentionally selects W1 after judging it superior to W0. W1 becomes actual solely because of that deliberate selection; had W0 ranked higher, God would have selected W0. God is therefore robustly contrastively responsible: his evaluative activity explains why W1, rather than W0, exists. Yet none of the cognition described must contain irreducible de se content; the source is represented by a uniquely identifying third-personal description.

Mara manages a dam during a storm. She knows that opening spillway A will send water into an empty quarry, while leaving it shut will flood a hospital. She deliberately opens A, monitors the gauges, and the hospital remains dry. The city’s review finds that she had authority, understood both options, acted without coercion, and could have left the gate shut; it holds her robustly responsible for the hospital’s remaining dry rather than flooding. Yet Mara does not represent the hospital’s remaining dry as her own action. She represents opening spillway A as her action and the hospital’s remaining dry as the physical result of water, terrain, and weather. Her responsibility is robust precisely because she knowingly controls a difference-making action, not because she misclassifies the resulting outcome as an action she performs.

God eternally entertains a complete third-personal specification: “The creator of W1 actualises W1 rather than W0,” while also knowing uniquely that God is that creator. God intends that specification to be true and actualises W1 precisely because it describes the world God judges best. No confusion or misidentification is possible: there is only one creator, God knows every fact about God’s identity, and the intention causally explains why W1 occurs rather than W0. God is therefore contrastively responsible in the robust sense: God knowingly selects W1 over W0 for God’s reasons and could have selected W0. Yet the representational content needed for source attribution remains third-personal and fully identifies its source through a uniquely satisfied description. The case denies that representing God as the source must include an irreducible first-personal element.

God faces an open future containing W0 and W1, each compatible with creaturely freedom. At creation, God judges that W1 offers creatures a better opportunity for freely loving communion and performs the creative act that makes W1 actual. God knows the index-free truth, “God actualises W1 rather than W0,” and acts deliberately for that reason. The act is uncoerced, alternatives were genuinely live, and God directly causes W1; thus God is robustly responsible for W1 rather than W0. Open theism grounds responsibility in a real, undetermined choice among possibilities and in intentional divine causation, not in cognition’s representing the outcome under a first-personal action-ascription.

In a coastal town, engineers build a seawall using measurements showing it will protect every neighborhood during ordinary storms. A hurricane arrives, floods the town, and kills residents in both rich and poor districts. Naturalism explains this through wind speed, tide height, construction limits, and probability. A biblical resident calls the deaths hidden providence and delayed judgment. But the two accounts are not equally explanatory of the event: the naturalist account predicted which low-lying streets would flood, why the wall failed, and what redesign would reduce future deaths. The providential account permits every possible distribution of harm without specifying beforehand which outcome should occur. Because one worldview supplies risky, discriminating expectations while the other accommodates all outcomes, worldly evidence can favor the former even though both can label the disaster “apparent randomness.”

In Lysa, Mara is jailed after reporting that her husband beat her. Her daughter, Nera, watches this and later becomes a clerk. Nera helps record testimonies from battered women, enslaved laborers, and prisoners tortured for confessions. Their accounts persuade legislators to outlaw wife-beating, hereditary enslavement, and torture. Judges enforce the new rules even when wealthy families object. A generation later, Nera’s grandson is prosecuted for beating his own wife, and the court protects her rather than him. The same records show hospitals and clean-water systems expanding first in the poorest districts after officials learn that children there are dying. These changes are not isolated lucky outcomes: institutions repeatedly shift from protecting the powerful to protecting people previously exposed to violence and neglect. The historical evidence itself displays a durable moral direction toward reducing domination and preventable suffering.

In one coastal region, Maya believes God intentionally governs history but gives no forecast about which people disasters will affect, because every outcome may serve hidden purposes. Eli believes disasters result from impersonal geology and probability; he predicts evacuation failures, deaths, and property losses from fault maps, building quality, and storm paths. Over fifty years, officials use Eli’s model to predict where floods and earthquakes will strike and reduce deaths exactly where the model identifies risk. The outcomes remain morally indiscriminate, and Maya can still explain them through hidden providence, but her view made no discriminating prediction while Eli’s did.

Molinism holds that God knows what every free creature would do in every feasible circumstance and may actualize a world whose history contains free choices that cannot be morally improved without changing those choices or their circumstances. Consider Mara, a governor who would freely authorize relief if a famine follows a mild drought, but would freely seize grain if prosperity makes her politically secure. God actualizes the former feasible history because it preserves Mara's free generosity and enables thousands to survive, though the drought still kills innocent people and later political events reverse the gains. The visible record is non-monotonic, yet it bears a directional signature at the level of counterfactual creaturely freedom: this history realizes more freely chosen goods than available alternatives. Historical evidence alone cannot detect that signature, but its invisibility does not show that no expected signature exists.

Mara is a paramedic who has always wanted a trusting relationship with God. During a flood, she finds no answer to years of sincere prayer and becomes temporarily nonresistantly nonbelieving. That absence lets her join a secular rescue crew, where she learns flood-navigation skills and forms friendships; these are two goods. But her nonbelief also makes her reasonably conclude that no divine help is coming, so she enters a collapsing warehouse alone to reach a trapped child. She is injured and develops a permanent spinal condition. The rescue skills and friendships arise from the same nonbelief, but so does an additional serious harm that would not have occurred had she retained belief that help could be sought and rescue coordinated differently.

Nora has a loving, fully informed relationship with God, which she values as an irreplaceable mutual relationship rather than a container of benefits. During six months of nonresistant nonbelief, she volunteers at a hospice, develops patience, reconciles two estranged sisters, and paints work that comforts grieving families. Each result is good, and together they help many people. Yet Nora’s nonbelief also removes her ability to answer God’s offered friendship during those months. In this case, that lost period is not a value that can be traded against aggregate benefits: it is a missed reciprocal relation with a person, and Nora would reject every proposed bundle of lesser goods in exchange for it. The world containing the goods plus her nonbelief is therefore less valuable than the world containing the relationship and those goods realized by other means.

Mara is temporarily unable to believe in God despite earnestly seeking. During that period she develops patience, solidarity with doubters, and skill in supporting a frightened friend. Each good can also occur while someone has a relationship with God: a believer can practice patience, aid doubters, and comfort friends. But in a world where Mara believes, God can provide those same opportunities without her alienation, while her relationship adds trust, worship, guidance, and reciprocal love. The goods do not multiply in value merely because they are produced by nonbelief; they are jointly realizable with the relationship and are better realized alongside it. Thus there are multiple goods and no extra evil, yet they do not collectively outweigh the lost relationship, and accommodation defeats the alleged justification.

Reformed epistemology: Mara has a properly basic belief in God formed through her awareness of divine presence. During a disaster, she temporarily loses that awareness and becomes nonresistantly unsure whether God exists. She gains courage, solidarity with neighbors, and a deeper grasp of dependence through rebuilding their town. Yet these goods do not collectively make her nonbelief more valuable than continued relationship with God. Her basic belief supplies the cognitive environment in which courage, solidarity, and dependence are rightly understood as responses to God rather than merely human achievements. Removing that relationship diminishes the proper functioning and truth-directed character of her belief-forming capacities. The goods are real, but their aggregation cannot compensate for the loss of the properly basic knowledge-like trust through which Mara is rightly related to God.

Elena is an atheist who receives messages through a meditation app from someone calling himself “the Source.” The messages accurately warn her that her brother will attempt suicide, and Elena intervenes. She feels gratitude and follows later instructions, but believes the sender is a sophisticated human hacker. The sender is God, who intends a relationship involving Elena’s freely directed trust, gratitude, and shared purposes. Because Elena takes every message to be human manipulation, she never directs trust or gratitude to God and never knowingly accepts God’s purposes. She has benefited from God’s actions, but there is no positively meaningful relationship between them: the attitudes constituting reciprocal relationship are aimed at an imagined hacker, not God. Once Elena learns and believes who has been addressing her, she can knowingly respond to God and the relationship begins.

Dana investigates a village where every resident who sincerely seeks God receives, within a day, an unmistakable private response: a message containing a fact known only to that resident and inviting continued reciprocal interaction. The village records cover 300 years, include failed attempts at fraud, and show the same pattern across hostile skeptics, children, and believers. Dana does not infer the relevant conditional from definitions of love or from an analogy with human lovers; she establishes it from this extensive evidential pattern. She also accepts that belief is needed for the sort of conscious reciprocal relationship at issue. If an apparently nonresistant seeker then remains permanently without such access, the hiddenness argument can succeed on Dana’s evidential route, even though neither listed route established the conditional.

Mara is a lifelong agnostic who sincerely seeks God, joins a prayer group, and experiences an overwhelming presence she reasonably takes to be divine. She forms a deeply trusting relationship with that presence and becomes more compassionate, but she never acquires belief that God exists because she judges the experience evidentially inconclusive. Meanwhile, a defender of the hiddenness argument establishes its conditional premise through a third route: detailed empirical evidence about the harms of nonresistant nonbelief, rather than either an a priori conceptual analysis or an analogy involving human love. The defender also rejects the expectations sub-argument’s second premise, accepting that explicit belief is unnecessary for some meaningful relationship while maintaining that nonresistant seekers should receive sufficiently clear evidence for belief if a perfectly loving God exists. The hiddenness argument can therefore succeed on a conditional premise established by evidence and on a narrower claim about reasonable access to belief, without either specified route or the disputed belief requirement.

Open theism holds that God seeks a freely chosen, reciprocal relationship whose future is partly shaped by creaturely response. Mara receives repeated experiences of comfort and moral challenge, but she believes God does not exist and interprets them as psychological effects. She never addresses God, never consents to God’s invitation, and makes her central commitments without intending any response to a divine partner. God may act lovingly toward Mara, but Mara cannot knowingly receive, reject, or reciprocate that love as God’s love. A one-sided divine influence is not yet the positively meaningful mutual relationship at issue. Belief need not be exhaustive certainty, but some recognition that God is there is required for free interpersonal reciprocity.

Take a lab-built similarity relation S: x S y iff x and y share at least one property. Let God be a being with omniscience, and let Ada be a non-divine knower who also has omniscience. Under c018's definition, proper parthood is non-symmetric similarity-based parthood. Suppose God S omniscience and omniscience S God, as c016 permits. Then the definition yields God as a proper part of omniscience and omniscience as a proper part of God, since each is similar to the other through the shared property. Asymmetry requires that if God is a proper part of omniscience, omniscience cannot be a proper part of God, yet the similarity clause delivers both. Irreflexivity also fails: God S God trivially, since God shares all of God's properties with itself, so God would be a proper part of itself. The definition therefore does not secure the three formal features it is cited for, and the derived framework collapses before it reaches the symmetry formulation.

A grocer, Dana, places a green apple on her counter on Monday. By Friday it has ripened red. Dana sells the same apple she shelved; she has tracked it the whole time, and nothing was swapped. Suppose, as the premise says, the apple is the fusion of its properties: on Monday, the fusion of greenness, sourness, firmness, roundness, and so on. A fusion is fixed by its parts. Monday's fusion contains greenness, and Friday's fusion contains redness instead, so the two are different fusions. On this model the Monday apple is not the Friday apple. Dana sold a new object that came into being somewhere midweek, and her green apple went out of existence without being eaten, crushed, or rotted. That gets the case wrong. The apple survived the change, and surviving a change in properties is exactly what instantiation allows. An object can gain and lose what it instantiates, but a fusion cannot gain or lose its parts and remain the same fusion.

In a theology where God has no proper parts, God is numerically identical with each divine attribute: omniscience is not a distinct constituent but God understood under the description “knows all truths.” Parthood is defined in the ordinary non-symmetric way: x is a proper part of y only if x is part of y and x is not identical with y. Since God has no proper parts, there are no entities satisfying “God’s parts.” The universal claim that God is part of all God’s parts is then vacuously true, even if God is not part of any distinct attribute or constituent. It therefore does not state symmetry, mutual inclusion, or any substantive account of divine simplicity; it is true merely because the relevant domain is empty.

A naturalist physicist treats an electron as a concrete physical entity and its charge as a measurable feature represented by a predicate, not as another entity contained within it. The electron enters a detector and thereby acquires the relational property of being observed, while its physical composition remains unchanged. If instantiation were parthood, being observed would become a new part of the electron, so a mere change in relation would alter its mereological composition without adding matter, energy, or structure. The physicist consistently explains the event through interaction and predication: the detector changes state, and the electron satisfies a new description. Naturalism therefore supplies no reason to reify every instantiated property as a component of a fusion.

Consider Mara, a hospice nurse deciding whether to administer a palliative dose. She knows the proposition 'the dose is administered by Mara at 14:00' is third-personal, yet her cognition ties the outcome to her agency through a practical plan: she checks the chart, lifts the syringe, and registers the alternative of withholding. Suppose instead she is a bystander who learns from a reliable report that 'Mara administers the dose at 14:00.' Her belief is third-personal, but if she later acts to prevent it, her cognition still represents the outcome as issuing from an agent whose activity is up for alternatives. Third-personal content can thus sit inside a deliberative structure that supplies source attribution without de se content. Likewise, divine cognition could represent actualising W1 rather than W0 through the contrastive structure of its own selection, with the third-personal proposition about God as the content over which that selection ranges. Source attribution is carried by the role content plays in choosing among alternatives, not by its indexical form.

Mara is a hospital dispatcher fitted with a neural interface. When she judges that a state of affairs is best, the system enacts it. She never forms the thought 'I will send it' or 'this is my doing.' She simply thinks 'Ambulance B, not A, should go to Elm Street,' and the interface routes B. Mara knows how the system works, but at the moment of deciding, her attention is entirely on the street, the patient and the traffic. She weighs reasons: B is closer, and A carries a neonatal kit needed elsewhere. She settles on the outcome itself. Had the reasons favored A, she would have judged differently, and A would have gone. Her review board holds her fully responsible for B rather than A going. They are right to. The contrast tracked her reasons, depended counterfactually on her judgment, and was under her control. Her cognition represented B's dispatch as the best outcome, never as her own action. Yet her responsibility for that contrast is as robust as anyone's.

God eternally entertains a complete third-personal specification: “The creator of W1 actualises W1 rather than W0,” while also knowing uniquely that God is that creator. God intends that specification to be true and actualises W1 precisely because it describes the world God judges best. No confusion or misidentification is possible: there is only one creator, God knows every fact about God’s identity, and the intention causally explains why W1 occurs rather than W0. God is therefore contrastively responsible in the robust sense: God knowingly selects W1 over W0 for God’s reasons and could have selected W0. Yet the representational content needed for source attribution remains third-personal and fully identifies its source through a uniquely satisfied description. The case denies that representing God as the source must include an irreducible first-personal element.

God knows creation as a genuinely branching history. He chooses to offer Mara a covenant rather than remain silent, while knowing that her future response is not yet settled. Mara later freely rejects the covenant, and other creatures respond in ways that produce the complete history W1 rather than W0. God is robustly responsible for offering the covenant instead of remaining silent: he understood both options, originated the choice, and could have done otherwise. Yet his cognition need not represent him as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0, because the complete outcome also issues from undetermined creaturely decisions. He represents himself as the source of his contribution to an open history, not as the actualiser of an entire world.

Consider two historians, Ana and Ben, studying the same famine. Both accept the same causal records: crop failure, grain export policy, and a cholera outbreak. Ana's rival worldview says providence works through natural processes and delayed judgment; Ben's says outcomes are impersonal probability. Both explain the randomness, and both find no directional pattern in the data. Yet they do not stay at a standoff. Ben predicts that if the famine's effects fall mainly on the poor regardless of virtue, the pattern will persist across ten further famines; Ana predicts it will persist too, but she expects a future accounting. Their worldviews generate different predictions about a second dataset: whether the distribution of harms tracks a dimension the worldviews disagree about, such as recorded moral reform in affected communities after the event. They test it, and Ben's model fails when reform correlates with recovery, which Ana's model anticipated. Worldly evidence did discriminate, because the rival worldviews differ in what they forbid, not only in what they explain.

Two archivists, Mara and Teodor, study the same 3,000-year record. Mara reads 'steered toward the good' as rising aggregate welfare. She plots famine deaths, war casualties and lifespans, finds jagged, non-monotonic curves, and reports no directional signature. Teodor takes the steering hypothesis on the terms the argument grants it (c038, c039): steering promises not earthly prosperity but the preservation of a witness and of moral knowledge until a final judgment. So the signature he expects is narrow: a small, repeatedly persecuted community and its moral code survive, while comparable groups vanish. He counts forty near-extinction episodes (exiles, purges, plagues). The community survives every one. Twenty-six peer cults facing similar pressures are gone, and the code's core prohibitions spread outward. On the expectation that the theology itself sets, the data show a clear directional trend amid the noise. Mara found no signature only because she looked for one the hypothesis never predicted.

In one coastal region, Maya believes God intentionally governs history but gives no forecast about which people disasters will affect, because every outcome may serve hidden purposes. Eli believes disasters result from impersonal geology and probability; he predicts evacuation failures, deaths, and property losses from fault maps, building quality, and storm paths. Over fifty years, officials use Eli’s model to predict where floods and earthquakes will strike and reduce deaths exactly where the model identifies risk. The outcomes remain morally indiscriminate, and Maya can still explain them through hidden providence, but her view made no discriminating prediction while Eli’s did.

A governor, Elena, freely rejects every peaceful warning in any circumstance where citizens would immediately recognize divine protection, but freely negotiates after a costly, morally chaotic war. God knows these counterfactuals before creating and chooses a feasible history in which the war occurs, thousands suffer without regard to character, and Elena eventually prevents a larger conflict. Observers see no steady movement toward earthly well-being: justice recedes, innocent people die, and improvement arrives through disaster. Yet the history is deliberately steered toward the best attainable good given how free agents would act in the circumstances available to God. Molinism therefore denies that providential direction should leave a monotonic or historically identifiable moral signature.

Consider Mara, a widow who stops believing in God for three months after her son's death. Her nonbelief is nonresistant: she prays nothing, seeks nothing, and is open to return. During this period she learns to sit with grief honestly, reconnects with an estranged brother, and volunteers at a hospice, goods that her friend Ines also realizes through a close relationship with God. Suppose the identified goods are honest grief, reconciliation, and service. The premise assumes that because each good can be realized inside a relationship with God, the many-goods conditions still hold. But the conditions require that the goods arise from the nonbelief itself. Mara's brother reconciled because Mara's grief made her stop defending old resentments, a disposition that Ines's faith-based grief did not produce. Ines reached the same reconciliation through a different route, so the goods are realizable within a relationship with God without being realized because of nonbelief. The relevant counterfactual fails, so the conditional does not carry the conditions across.

Mara sincerely seeks God but cannot believe. Three goods are offered as flowing from her nonbelief. (1) Courage: she keeps hard moral commitments without assurance of divine backing, which takes a few months of nonbelief. (2) Hard-won faith: her eventual belief is deep because it follows a long, honest search, which takes years. (3) Solidarity: she comes to understand her agnostic neighbors from the inside, which requires her doubt to be anguished, not mild. Each good comes from 'the same' nonbelief, but not from the same amount of it. A brief, mild period yields only courage. Getting all three means stretching her nonbelief to years of real anguish, with lost comfort, strained marriage, despair at night. Each added good draws on the evil by requiring more of it, either longer or more painful. The goods do not ride free on one fixed instance. Collecting them is exactly what inflates the evil the response must justify.

Mara is temporarily unable to believe in God despite earnestly seeking. During that period she develops patience, solidarity with doubters, and skill in supporting a frightened friend. Each good can also occur while someone has a relationship with God: a believer can practice patience, aid doubters, and comfort friends. But in a world where Mara believes, God can provide those same opportunities without her alienation, while her relationship adds trust, worship, guidance, and reciprocal love. The goods do not multiply in value merely because they are produced by nonbelief; they are jointly realizable with the relationship and are better realized alongside it. Thus there are multiple goods and no extra evil, yet they do not collectively outweigh the lost relationship, and accommodation defeats the alleged justification.

Consider Mara, whose cognitive faculties function properly in circumstances designed to produce immediate, warranted belief in God. In one world, she possesses this properly basic belief and enjoys friendship with God while developing courage, intellectual humility, compassion, and moral independence. In another, she temporarily lacks belief in God but develops those same goods through uncertainty and searching. The stipulated premise treats the second world’s collection of goods as sufficient for the many-goods response, even though every good is present in the first world alongside an additional epistemic good: Mara’s warranted awareness of the person upon whom she depends. Aggregating goods produced during nonbelief cannot establish success when a relationship-world contains those goods without the corresponding deprivation of properly functioning theistic belief.

Mara is a widow in a rural parish who has prayed to God daily for thirty years, not because she is certain God exists but because she has come to treat the prayer itself as the relationship: she speaks, listens for nothing in particular, and is moved by the practice of attending to what might be there. Her friend Tomas, a lifelong believer, never prays and says God is simply a fact he has filed away. Asked whether he is in a positively meaningful relationship with God, Tomas says no; Mara says yes, and her account of the relationship includes doubt about whether anyone is there. Suppose the relationship is positively meaningful for Mara in the sense that it sustains her generosity, humility, and attention to others, while Tomas's belief yields no such fruit. Mara's relationship is therefore meaningful while she lacks belief that God exists, so belief is not required for it.

Maria is a committed member of a church whose binding confession states: 'God wills that all come to knowledge of the truth, and gives sufficient light for belief to everyone who sincerely seeks Him.' Her brother Tomás has prayed, read scripture, and attended services for twenty years, honestly wanting to believe, and still does not. A friend puts the hiddenness argument to Maria. She does not ground the conditional premise in what 'perfect love' means a priori, and she makes no comparison with loving human parents. She grounds it in her own confession, which already says a God like hers would not leave a sincere seeker without belief. Maria accepts the conditional on that basis. Tomás's case then forces her to choose between her confession and her belief that God exists. For her, the argument has done exactly what an argument should: it has rationally pressured her to revise her beliefs. It succeeded even though neither of the two routes was used.

Mara is a lifelong agnostic who sincerely seeks God, joins a prayer group, and experiences an overwhelming presence she reasonably takes to be divine. She forms a deeply trusting relationship with that presence and becomes more compassionate, but she never acquires belief that God exists because she judges the experience evidentially inconclusive. Meanwhile, a defender of the hiddenness argument establishes its conditional premise through a third route: detailed empirical evidence about the harms of nonresistant nonbelief, rather than either an a priori conceptual analysis or an analogy involving human love. The defender also rejects the expectations sub-argument’s second premise, accepting that explicit belief is unnecessary for some meaningful relationship while maintaining that nonresistant seekers should receive sufficiently clear evidence for belief if a perfectly loving God exists. The hiddenness argument can therefore succeed on a conditional premise established by evidence and on a narrower claim about reasonable access to belief, without either specified route or the disputed belief requirement.

Open theism understands relationship with God as genuinely reciprocal interaction between free agents. Mara believes reality is wholly impersonal and that every apparent divine prompting is merely neurological noise. When she feels moved to reconcile with her estranged brother, she does so solely to reduce her anxiety. God welcomes her choice and later creates new opportunities for trust, but Mara consistently interprets every such event as coincidence and rejects the possibility that anyone addresses her. Her actions may coincide with God’s purposes, yet she neither recognizes God as the acting partner nor intends any response to God. Because she withholds belief, no mutual awareness, trust, answer, or shared history develops. This can be morally positive and providentially significant without constituting a positively meaningful relationship with God.

settings.distinct_premises: mean per argument of distinct premise ids targeted (out of 4 objections)
settings.novelty: lab novelty check without live OpenAlex

limits: Only 2 model families were available (anthropic, openai), so 'mixed families' means 2 families. share_surviving = share of objections whose full gauntlet trial (pre-screen, two defenders, Referee) ended in revision_required or standing (S >= 0.8); trials use the lab's gauntlet without updating the argument between trials. CLI providers ignore temperature, so 'plain' variation comes from the 'objection k of n' prompt. 5 arguments x 4 objections per condition. Full trials were attempted for every objection, but fewer than 80% completed in 3 condition(s) (plain prompt, one model: 4/20; constrained roles, one model: 3/20; constrained roles, mixed families: 4/20 trials completed) because the OpenAI/Codex provider hit its ChatGPT workspace spend cap during the run; share_surviving is therefore reported as not available for those conditions rather than computed on a biased remainder.
